projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Raymond R. Jorz was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II and Korean war veteran Raymond R. Jorz. Mr. Jorz served on the U.S. Marine Corps with the First Marine Division, Fifth Marine Regiment, Second Battalion. He served in the Pacific Theater during World War II and Korea. His highest rank was colonel. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Jorz's home in metro Ohio on September 23rd, 2003. The noise you hear in the background is a rather noisy rainstorm. Ray was 78 at the time of this recording. [The interview was transcribed and processed by Brandy M. Collins]. SWOPE: When did you join the Marines? JORZ: February 10th, 1943. I was turning 18 on February the 11th, and I wanted to get into a service so that I could make my choice of military organizations rather than have the draft board do it for me. And I was going to enlist in the Navy first, but the paperwork was overwhelming. Went to a marine recruiter at public square and told him I wanted to join the Marine Corps. He handed me one sheet of paper and says, "Here, fill this out, bring it back tomorrow." And he looked at me; he says, "You're not 18 yet, are you?" And I said, "No." He says, "Give this form to your father and have him fill it out, and bring those two back tomorrow, and we'll enlist you." And that's the way it was. {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were able to enlist before you were 18?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: That's right. At 17 you needed -- you needed a guardian's consent. Right. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you went in in '43?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me what you can about your basic training.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Well, that was boot camp, Parris Island. Probably the easiest stint I had in the Marine Corps. As a matter of fact, I didn't necessarily enjoy it, but I found it not to be overwhelming and it was made very, very simple because the drill instructor told you precisely what to do, when to do it, and how to do it. And all you had to do was say, yes, sir. And that was the end of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything unusual happen during that time?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Not really. Typical boot camp: Cold, windy. A record day was a cold, windy day, and unfortunately -- well, I did, I did qualify. But other than that, no, it was a typical thing. I came out of boot camp as a PFC and then went off to Camp Lejeune for further training.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your advance training then at Camp Lejeune?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Advance infantry training. We -- we learned how to walk farther and faster and carry more gear. {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So your specific job was a rifleman?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Rifleman, yeah. Rifleman. Right. Exactly. And that's what I basically wanted to do: Be -- be a member of the queen of battles I guess, huh? Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you always want to be a marine even before when you were -- ___+

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh, no. Not at all. Matter of fact, my brother was -- at that time -- was in the Navy and I wanted to be -- be in the Navy just as he was. And the thing that got me into the Marine Corps was I was a freshman at West Reserve University as a premed, and the recruiters came to the area, and one of them was a marine, and he was sharp, and his forest green uniform really stood out among the rest. And basically that's the first time I think I'd ever seen a marine and a marine officer. I think he was a first lieutenant or a captain. And then that's what brought back that came to my mind when I was sitting at home filling out those Navy recruitment papers. And I thought, well, the Marines sound like a good deal. And it turns -- as it turns out, it was. They were. Right. We were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Backtracking a bit, do you have specific memories of the day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It was a Sunday, late Sunday afternoon, yeah. I was a senior in high school. And, yeah, at -- and I remember we lived in an old neighborhood on Sowinski and Ansel Road. And I remember my brother and sister-in-law lived in the suite above us and in the home we shared -- they paid rent, of course. And I remember going upstairs and saying to them, "The Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor." And they were aghast. And the reality of it really didn't sink in until the following day when I listened on the radio to President Roosevelt's address to joint members of congress, and talked about the day of infamy. That's when it really settled in, the following day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, do you remember doing anything at high school or the time before you went in the Marines for the war effort?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: No. No. It was -- we -- we were, of course, Pearl Harbor in 1941. I graduated in June of '42, so actually there was not really much to do or to think about. Excepting that every once in a while a Cathedral Latin graduate got into the news as a -- as a hero, or as a member of the services, and that was about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So then you took a job I assume after you graduated for a short while --

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- before you got enlisted?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: I went to work at Warner and Swayze making turret lathes. And I had a pretty decent job and made enough money that year to pay for my tuition at Western Reserve University. And I even went to the May Company and bought a real snazzy outfit to wear on campus, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: But, yeah, at 65 cents an hour -- and I don't know what the credit hours were back in those days at Western Reserve, but they weren't more like than two or three dollars a credit hour versus two or three hundred or more a credit hour today. {Laughs} Yeah. So I made enough money to pay for my full year of freshman year at Reserve.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. Let's get back to where we were before. Where did you go after Camp Lejeune?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: As a matter of fact, at Camp Lejeune we were standing in formation and the NCO's and officers began to call out names. And they call out my name, and they said, "Okay. Go get your gear and your sea bag and stand over there." We ended up then going to an officer candidate applicant formation at Camp Lejeune, and we stayed there for, I don't know, two or three months, and then eventually ended up at Quantico in OCS, and ultimately was commissioned to second lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about OCS? I don't believe I've talked to anybody about -- ___

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: {Laughs} OCS was -- oh, was magnificently horrible. It was magnificent because we succeeded. But it was -- it was a horrible episode. At that time -- prior to the time our arrival at Quantico -- Officer Candidate School consisted of two ten-week sessions. First ten-week session was OCS, and then you were commissioned to second lieutenant, then you went to ten more weeks of what they called ROS reserve officers. We were all reserves at that time, reserve officer training. When I got to Quantico, the need for second lieutenants was so significantly great that they took the course and compressed it. They took the 20-week course, compressed it into 16 weeks, and did not leave out a single item out of the syllabus. So we essentially worked six or seven days a week from 0700 first classroom, and we had evening classes that generally got out at 9 o'clock, so we worked, and that was -- that was the drudgery of it. Once in a while, we got a late Saturday afternoon off. Sundays were generally off. But late afternoon -- and once in a while we managed to get into -- get the train from Quantico into DC for a weekend of liberty. And hopefully somebody had a hotel room that you could {laughs} share with 23 other guys.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs} What'd you do when you went on liberty on those rare occasions?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh, just enjoyed the -- the freedom, the expanse of Washington, DC, the beauty of it, the significance of it. One of my buddies was a guy named Luke Gross (ph), who -- who was not in my class but was in an adjoining class. So we met one afternoon, late afternoon, and just on a whim decided to go to Washington. A train was there so we jumped on a train, got into DC, got off the train station, and across from union station somewhere close by was the Washington Hotel, as I remember. So we went to the hotel and attempted to get a room. And of course we kept -- the desk clerk laughed at us and he says, are you crazy? Wartime -- wartime rooms were impossible to get. So we didn't know what we were going to do with ourselves. So we started to walk out the lobby, and a -- a bell captain came by, and he had a little pad in his hand, and he wrote on the pad, do you want a room? And we -- and we nodded, yes. He says, five-dollar tip. So we gave him a five-dollar tip and we had a room.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: And so we hit the bar, maybe, and of course I was 20 years old at the time. I wasn't even legally able to drink, but there was not much of a problem if you had a uniform. So we kind of wandered around and had dinner and then came back and the following morning, we had breakfast and -- Luke knew Washington, DC, pretty well. His parents were -- were out of Shaker Heights and they did a lot of traveling. And so we had lunch at one of the really nice Washington hotels -- restaurants. As a matter of fact, he ordered a shrimp cocktail, and I did the same thing, and that was the first time I'd ever tasted -- so anyhow, we left and we had to get the train back to Quantico. So we're walking down the street. And we stopped at an intersection, and a nice big, black limousine pulls up at the traffic light. The window rolls down and Mrs. Eleanor Roosevelt pokes her head out the window and says, "Good morning, boys." And we said -- shocked in disbelief -- we said -- we retorted with a, "Good morning, ma'am." And then the light changed and the window went up, and off she drove. So I guess that was my most memorable experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: And out of Quantico and out of everywhere else. We almost didn't make it because that was the case with everybody else. The training was rigorous and the supervision was even more so. Supervision was superb and we had to stay on our toes literally all the time. The guy who was my company -- or platoon leader at that time -- was a first lieutenant named Paul Sanders (ph) who had been on Guadalcanal. And so we looked up to him and respected him. His stature was not magnificent because I think he stood about five foot six, five foot seven maybe at the most, and probably weighed about a hundred and thirty-five pounds. He was a -- he was a nice guy, a real good guy, and he helped us, and we had a name for him. We called him Mighty Mouse, but never to his face. As it turns out, I met Paul Sanders about ten years ago, and for the very first time, and -- and looked at him and didn't really recognize him. He aged somewhat. But I did look at him, and I did ultimately recognize him, and I came up to him and I said, "Hey, I was in your platoon leaders class at Quantico back in" -- whatever the time was. And I -- he looked at me, he says, "Well, I -- I don't remember you," he says. But, he says, "Prove to me that you were in that class." And I said, "Well, I -- I -- I can." He said, "Yeah." He says, "Well one proof is, what do you guys -- what did you guys call me behind my back?" And I said, "We called you Mighty Mouse." And he says, "You're it." He says, "I remember you now. Okay."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: And that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: For the most part, did you get along with your superior officers?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh, you had to. Ha. And particularly in the Marine Corps. If they're -- if they're -- as a matter of fact, your superior officer in boot camp was a PFC. Your superior officer in, later in life was, of course, a second lieutenant on up. But yes, it was a yes, sir; no, sir; on my way up, how high do you want me to jump, sir? You know. Right. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So then what happened next after OCS?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: We went out to Camp Pendleton for some more training. And then I ended up with a Fleet Marine Force, Pacific, FMFPac, and I ended up on Guam. And I was a, what they called, a -- an office pogue. I ended up as a dispatch officer and a, oh -- oh, an officer messenger. I was literally a -- really an office pogue, a real -- a real -- a real pinky. My job was to review all of the -- from the ___ Command Guam -- to review all of this dispatches that were -- that came in, and to route them out to the proper areas, handle top secret information, deliver messages in person to Admiral Nimitz (ph) who was a ___ who was running the Pacific War from that point. Although I never got to see the admiral because I could never get past his flag secretary. But I did things like that when the -- when the dispatches came in, usually by air, I went to the airfield and picked them up and sorted them out. And they had an extremely top secret communications facility on Guam, and once in a while I had to go into that area and -- and send out some messages and encode and so on and so on. But that was my job. And then I -- after that I stayed there through the end of the war, came back and was discharged. And I was discharged with my permanent rank which was platoon sergeant. At that time, all the commission warrants were all temporary warrants. But my permanent job was platoon sergeant. So I was discharged with that. And then I was allowed to sign a paper, and I stayed in the reserve. When I got back to Cleveland, there was an organized reserve unit that was -- that was formed. And I think a year or two after that, I think I finally graduated from college. And after that I joined the reserve unit, which was the Seventh Infantry Battalion, which ultimately became mobilized on August 22, 1950, because the previous June the North Koreans decided that they wanted South Korea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let me make sure I've got the dates right. When did you get to Guam?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Got to Guam right --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it in '45?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: No. It was -- I can't remember the exact date -- it was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, you know the date's not -- generally was it -- ___+

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: It was -- yeah, it was somewhere around '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Right. Yeah. Yeah. Probably about January, I would guess. January, February. Right. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So then call to active service --

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: In August 22nd, 1950. We were married -- I was married on June 18th, 1949. And we were scheduled to go to camp -- to go back to Camp Pendleton. And that was it. As a matter of fact, {laughs} you mentioned Lin Mar (ph). Lin, when he was discharged from the Marine Corps, came and lived in Cleveland. The Koreans invaded, I think, on June 26th of 1950. Lin was married on June 25th of 1950. And Lin, by some chance, joined that same reserve unit that I was in. And so in August of 1950, Lin was activated too. He and his new bride ended up out at -- out at Camp Pendleton in California. They lived in -- same as we did -- we were -- I took my wife with me -- my wife, eventually, with me. We lived in San Clemente and, well, because the back gate to Camp Pendleton was really close to the city of San Clemente, so we were able to -- and we were in what they called tent camp two -- so we were able to get back into the back gate without too much trouble. And it was a relatively short distance of travel.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what kind of training did they give you when you went -- were called back to active service?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Ha-ha. Mountain warfare. We climbed mountains and with full packs and full gear, and we were up and down. It was basically conditioning because at that particular time, one of the intelligence reports that was -- that was coming -- were coming -- which were coming back to us was that the -- one of the reasons the North Koreans weren't able to overrun American forces were they were out of shape. They -- they weren't -- they didn't maintain a high level of physical training, and so they -- they made us -- they made us pretty good examples of what good fitness should be in a -- in a camp combat zone. Yeah. So we marched and marched and marched. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long did that take --

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Not too long.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- training take?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: We got there in probably the first part of September, and within a few weeks they began to form replacement drafts. We had found a nice house in San Clemente. My wife -- my wife and my buddy's wife found a nice two-bedroom house in San Clemente that they rented, thinking we'd be there for a few months. Well, about a week after that, we came home -- she and I came home -- and there's Al and his wife, and they're hugging each other and they're in tears because Al is leaving tomorrow morning, flying out in the first replacement draft and heading to Korea, because at that particular time, the landing at Inch’on was being formed, and he was going to become a member of the Inch’on landing. And again, he was going to be flown over, and so it wasn't very long, and about a week after that the second replacement draft was ordered to San Diego to board ships and -- and head out to Japan where we outfitted and ultimately then immediately to Korea. Al landed at Inch’on a few weeks later, several weeks later I guess it was, maybe a month later. Maybe not even that long. We landed at Wonson over on the opposite coast, and then headed up north and joined the -- joined the First Marine Division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what can you tell me about that experience? What was your first day in combat like?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Well, first day in combat, I was pretty remote. The fir- -- because there were other units who were -- who were doing the fighting. But where we landed in Wonson -- I guess it was a kind -- in a kind -- in a kind of a combat zone because there still -- were still a few guerrillas who were operating around, but they gave me the charge of a ammunition fuel train to be taken from Wonson up to the port of Hamhung, which is close to where the First Marine Division was. So we took this fuel train up, and we were going through a territory that was basically occupied by guerrillas, and so we were warned very specifically if the train stops, or if you see anything, you know, you always point ?odd board? And we were a little concerned because among things -- among the things we had had on that train was aviation gas, diesel fuel, artillery rounds. And I'm not sure what else, so -- but we did make it to -- we did get up to Hamhung, and then we went up to -- up to Koto-ri where I joined the First Marine Division. And then after that, the Fir- -- Fifth -- Fifth Marine Division was kind of in reserve because of Seventh Marine -- Seventh Marine -- ___ Fifth Marine Regiment was in reserve because the Seventh Marines were up front. When we got close to Hungnam, which is the area that the Chinese came in on the 27th of November of 1950, Fifth Marines leapfrogged across the Seventh Marines lines, and soon the -- the attack to the north. At that particular time, I was in charge of a 60 millimeter mortar section, so I was kind of in reserve, kind of out of -- out of it pretty much. But not for long because the first platoon leader was hit by a sniper and the company commander then motioned to me. He says, you, there. So I took over the first platoon and we laid -- and we set down. We made an attack and at nighttime we formed our lines. My platoon tied in with Fox Company which occupied a hill on our left. We stretched across an area which was -- which -- which became known as Easy -- Easy Alley, or Easy Valley. It was a wide expanse, and I tied in with the second platoon on my right and so on down the line. And then on that night the Chinese decided they were going to undo our -- our forward movement.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So describe that night -- if -- whatever you remember from that night.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Well, my platoon leader and I set our people out on a line and we had a -- a machine gun section, two machine guns attached to us so we put them out in front of us. So my platoon sergeant and I found a nice little -- really nice little area close to a stream, and although the temperatures were freezing or below freezing, there was still some movement in the stream, so we had fresh water which was kind of a rarity because you were eating snow most of the time. So we ___ out in our sleeping bags and about an hour later, and it became -- when it became completely dark, the machine gun began to fire. And I had my phone inside my bag and the company commander rang me up and says, "What the hell's going on over there?" And I said, "I don't know, skipper." He says, "Well," he says, "knock off the machine gun fire and kill them with your rifles." So I dutifully yelled from my sleeping bag, "Knock off the machine gun fire and kill them with your rifles and try to get back to sleep again." But ten minutes later the stuff hit the fan, and the Chinese swarmed in all over the place. So we zoomed out of our bags and reassembled -- or formed our -- reformed our lines and got our people back into position, and the machine guns were firing away, and every fourth round on a machine gun is a -- is a tracer, an incendiary round. And about an hour into the battle, that incendiary round ignited a farmhouse which was up in the valley, maybe about a thousand yards from our position. Now, the typical Korean farmhouse consisted of living quarters for people and living quarters for the livestock. And, of course, the livestock had all the hay and all the other stuff in it, so when that tracer round hit that farmhouse, it ignited it and ignited the valley so that literally we were able -- from our position, I was halfway up the hill. From our position up the hill, we were able to see these hordes of advancing Chinese coming at us and we had -- they were in -- in -- in full white. We were able to literally see who we were shooting at and we -- when we -- if you hit them, you can see them fall, and so that farmhouse stayed ignited probably for a half hour. And the Chinese eventually were -- we -- were beaten back so they scurried back and -- and -- and didn't bother us the rest of the night. And the Fox Company position on top of our hill was taken over by Chinese, so the following morning I -- and they sent me over a reenforcement of another platoon, so I and the platoon leader plotted our attack, and we decided we were going to take that hill at first light. So I set his platoon up as a base of fire and as light first came, he began to fire and I said, "Okay. We're going to attack up the hill, and as soon as we start throwing grenades, you stop the firing." So that's basically the way it was. We went up, we took the hill, and -- and that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that was the first night of the attack --

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah, that's it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- of November 26th?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: November 27th.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah. Temperatures eventually got down to about 30 below and -- and -- so we -- we took the hill, and we could look down into the valley where our company was, and there was still a lot of firing and shooting going on, so I sent a runner down and -- and check with the company commander and see if he needs some help. The runner never did come back, and eventually I said I'm going to go down on my own, and I started going down the hill. And apparently somebody tossed a mortar shell or a grenade, and that was the end of me. So I slid on my butt down the way -- the rest of the way down the hill. Ended up in the Battalion Aid Station and stayed with the column. See, the Marines then decided to stay together, and the Fifth Marines and the Seventh Marines joined up at that point and decided that the only way, the best way, to get out was to stay together as a consolidated unit and to fight our way back, back to the sea, back to the port of Hamhung which we -- which was -- one -- one place we were at originally. The First Marine Regiment was south of us about 20 miles so they fought their way up north. And so our division commander negated the suggestions, or the orders, of the superior army people who said, "When you get down to Hagaru, there's a airstrip that's chiseled out of the ground." Said, "We want you to take your Marines and we'll fly them out. Leave all your equipment behind, leave your dead behind, but fly out." And General O.P. Smith said, "No way." He says, "We're going out like Marines." Hagaru was an airstrip where the wounded were flown out of it and I was a lone man and ended up getting flown out at Hagaru, which was about 20, 25 miles south of Yudam-ni where the Chinese originally came in -- came into the picture.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were your injuries when you were wounded?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: I had shrapnel wounds in my left chest and side and was eventually flown into somewhere south of the -- south -- middle of Korea somewhere and then picked up -- picked up on an airplane and flown into Fukuoka, Japan, where we boarded a hospital train and were -- were trans- -- transported over to Yokosuka Naval Hospital and so we stayed there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long did it take to recover?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Well, the hospital became very full of very seriously combat-injured people. A great deal of frostbite. A lot of frostbite. They opened a hospital annex in a little town called Otsu where we first came, where we were outfitted for -- with cold weather gear and then shipped off to Korea from Otsu. So that's where they opened the hospital annex and they took the ambulatory people, and I was one of them, and -- and -- and shipped us down to Otsu, and we stayed there for two, three weeks. Matter of fact, it was right after the first of the year sometime. And Otsu was very close to Kyoto and so the liberty wasn't bad since we were ambulatory. Three or four of us could jump into a Japanese taxicab for a few yen, and the rate of exchange was superb at that time. And -- and -- enjoy the town of Kyoto. So I -- and I stayed there and I had a physical examination that morning and the doctor says, "You can go back to duty in two weeks." And about that time, a dispatch came from headquarters of the Marine Corps saying, we need people back in the States for training purposes. Anybody with a hospital stay of 14 days or more will be given orders and be transported back to the States immediately. And that's -- that's what happened with me. So we got back and got back to Cleveland and I was given orders to report to Parris Island, South Carolina, for training with the recruit depot. And at that time I had a wife who was very pregnant. I stayed home as long as I could but she would not deliver. I stay -- I think I had leave coming until sometime around early April. So I reported to Parris Island. Shortly thereafter, I received a telephone call from her brother saying that I was the father of a -- of a young baby boy born on May 3rd of 1950 and ___+ --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '51 you mean?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: '51 rather. Yeah. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: So we stayed in Parris Island for a couple of years and then ultimately I got out of the -- out of the active duty role.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So how long were you in Korea then?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: I was in Korea probably for about six weeks. I think probably from -- yeah -- about earl- -- about mid -- yeah, probably from about sometime early October until November 28th when I was wounded. And ultimately I think I flew out of Hagaru on December 4th or 5th, one of those days. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You got any close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh, sure. Still have a few. Yeah. A lot of guys from the Cleveland unit over there. And one of the things that came as a result of Korea was a -- a fraternal organization who were known as the Chosin Few. We who survived the Korean March, or the Korean -- we don't call that a retreat, but the Korean Evacuation have become members of the Chosin Few. It's a national organization and there are very local chapters. For example, we were heading back to Florida, probably sometime around the 8th or 9th of October. And we're close to Cape Coral, and Cape Coral is a home of Wally Dugan, who is a warrant officer, a good friend of mine, who is president of the Southwest Florida Chapter of the Chosin Few. So we have regular meetings and a lot of camaraderie and a lot of -- not a lot of -- but a number of regional meetings. For example, last week, about two weeks ago, the -- the Georgia Chapter of the Chosin Few had a meeting in Albany, Georgia. And they invite the Florida people, and the Florida people get invited to the -- to the other side by the Texas Chosin Few members. So we have a number of small regional meetings where we have maybe two or three hundred in attendance, and we get to know each other pretty well, and those kind of meetings are generally very -- very -- very pleasant, very successful and informative. And we usually take wives with us and the wives are -- she's the auxiliary -- member of the Auxiliary Chapter of the Southwest Florida Chapter. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies during that six weeks over there?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah. Yes. Guys that I had in my reserve platoon, in particular, guys that we knew from other reserve units. Oh, yeah. Yes. Guys like -- well -- yes, we did. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: One of the questions we always like to ask. You were there for six weeks. I don't know, how often does it happen? Memories of mail call.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I got -- I got mail. Not very much because I wasn't there long enough for the mail to really catch up to me but eventually it did -- but, yes, she was a good writer. As a matter of fact, you talk about mail call, one of the things that --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: -- one of the things that saved my butt I think was the fact that I had a packet of stationary in my left chest pocket, combat stationary. And it basically was a little kit that consisted of about 20 sheets of writing paper and about 20 envelopes. And that was in my left breast pocket. And when I got hit, a piece of shrapnel was -- was coming into from my left chest area, hit that packet first, and then was deflected off of a metal button on my parka so that the full impact of that round wasn't felt by me, and I think it probably saved my life. Because it could have -- it could have gotten further. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, mail call. Oh, yeah, great. She sent me one of her gorgeous pictures which I carry, still carry in my wallet. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A little cheesecake, or -- {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Kinda. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was your reunion when you finally got back stateside? What was your reunion like?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: It was superb because when we got to Treasure Island, San Francisco, we were -- we were processed, given physicals, and then processed. And I was one of the early ones and so I -- had -- was able to make airplane reservations and I got to -- I can't remember the date that I got back to Cleveland, but I think I was about one of the first guys back. We were transported by ship from Japan to San Francisco, and there must have been a thousand Marines aboard, most of them frostbite, a lot of wounded, so I was able to get back pretty early. And as a matter of fact, as I debarked from the airplane, the Cleveland press photographer was there and took our picture. And with the quote, hey -- you know, glad to be home or whatever it was. And, yeah, it was superb. It was a superb homecoming. As a matter of fact, prior to my getting called up in the reserve, I was a teacher of biology and science at Cathedral Latin High School. And her mother was the cafeteria manager, and she was the one who got us together in the first place way back -- but anyhow, the publicity -- the publicity that we got generated further publicity and one -- one afternoon, we were living -- living with her mother on -- on 80th street in -- in Cleveland. A knock on the door and a couple of Cleveland firemen were there and they were representatives of the St. Patrick's Day parade in Cleveland that particular year, March 17th, and the banquet that followed. So they invited us to become the grand -- honorary grand marshals of the St. Patrick's Day parade. And so we did. So we -- and it was held at the old Holland hotel which was close to 9th and Superior. And, yeah, I was -- say, being the first to return, I did get a lot of notoriety. And as a matter of fact, I appeared one Sunday afternoon on the Dorothy Fuldheim news show. You remember Dorothy Fuldheim?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I sure do.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: A prominent female redheaded newscaster. So, yeah. And one of the -- one of the -- you talked about losing friends and good people, the Downing Brothers. I enlisted in the Marine Corps because one of my stints during my reserve training was recruiting duty. So I enlisted the Downing Brothers into the Marine Corps and they ended up in Korea. And when I got back home, they were among the people listed as missing. And Mrs. Downing called me on the phone and pleafully inquired, "You know, do you know anything about my boys?" And I said, "No." I said, "As far as I know they're still missing. But pray the fact that the missing is a good sign rather than KIA." Well, ultimately they were -- they were captured by Chinese and did die in a Chinese prisoner-of-war camp. They were both perished. And, yeah, that was one of the sad tales that a recruiter has to face. You know, you sign them up and then you lose them. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience in Korea, does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: No. That was probably it. That -- that's about as vivid as you can get. We were in a column as we were marching out. The Marines took care of us. We were wounded. We stayed in a column. We were protected by the Marines. And the most notable factor was 30 below zero temperatures. Somehow you manage to try to keep warm and you try to -- try to save your butt in any way that you could. Oh. Yeah. One of the things, you know, the -- the night that the Chinese came in, some of the troopers from Fox Company came running down the hill, and they were caught in their sleeping bags. And this one kid in particular, I remember, came running down the hill and he was barefooted. He had the rest of his gear on him, his parka and -- and the whole bit, and he's running down the hill barefooted, and I grabbed him, and I said, "Where are you going?" I said, "Where are your boots?" He says, "They're up there with the Chinese." So one of the things that we were issued were woolen mittens with a -- a canvas cover. So I pulled my gloves off, and I pulled off the woolen mitten part, and I handed them to them -- him. And I said, "Okay. At least put these on your feet, and then when you got to the bottom of the hill, God help you." You know. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. We were caught in sleeping bags because the Chinese came in unexpectedly. We never expected it. Although we knew they were in the area because I had gone out on numerous patrols looking for them. But the Chinese were superbly disciplined, superbly trained during the daytime. They hid out -- they -- no motion, no movement, and particularly no fire. And the Chinese uniforms were nowhere near the quality that ours were so these people survived, and amazingly, amazingly. So I stayed in the reserve and the active duty and reserve for over 30 years. So, and again, I'm retiring. And the nice part about it is I'm strong enough and hale and hearty enough and around to draw some of the benefits of that previous service. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: I hope so. Hey, I can't think of anything other -- much more significant. Excepting that the camaraderie of the Chosin Few was very, very significant. And -- and -- again, the Marines prove themselves to be Marines where extreme Marine Regiments combine far off probably a hundred and fifty to 200,000 Chinamen -- Chinamen. We had a force probably of around 15,000. Of course, one of the grand things that occurred in Korea, we not only fought together, we fought well together. But we had air support from the Navy and from our own Marine pilots, and the air support probably was very exceedingly significant in terms of our being able to get back out. We flew out of -- I flew out of Hagaru. The unit fought its way down to the port of Hungnam and eventually boarded LSTs which took them back to Japan, some of them -- or back down to South Korea where they reformed again. But among the notable things that occurred in that evacuation in Hungnam, we probably took out about a hundred thousand Koreans who were fleeing for their lives and -- and took them down to South Korea. So, yeah, the Marines -- the Marines are one hell of a unit, and if there weren't a Marine I probably wouldn't be here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have much contact with the South Koreans when you were over there?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Well, yeah. Well, very little South Koreans because I ended up almost immediately in the port of Wonson which is in North -- part of North Korea. We had with us generally our -- each platoon had a couple of Koreans that were assigned to us as -- as interpreters and as -- or guides, yes. So that -- basically my contact with South Koreans were with a couple of South Korean military guys. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about any North Korean civilians -- ___+

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Very few. The most significant thing I remember about a North Korean, we were standing on a hill one time and it was close to Thanksgiving time and the temperatures were a -- a balmy, probably, 20 -- 20 degrees Fahrenheit. But I remember this little Korean boy who was dressed in very, very scanty cotton clothing, who was just standing there and shivering and watching us as we marched off, off to the wars. So the civilians were the sufferers, and again, that impression of that little kid standing there. Hopefully he made it, but who knows.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: That's it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Think we got it?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: I don't know. What do you think?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is kind of for you left to say, whatever you want to say -- ___+ [Interviewer, Veteran, and Unidentified Speaker begin talking over one another for approximately 30 seconds].

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Well, there are a lot of things that you did that you seem to forget.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: {Laughs} Fortunately I came out and --

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: -- with the notes ___+

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: But some things that I, you know, do impress you. And I think another thing worth mentioning certainly are the -- the Navy paramedics -- they don't call them paramedics --

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh, our corpsmen.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Corpsmen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Corpsmen.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: The corpsmen were magnificent.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh. The corpsmen were superb actually.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: And the Navy corpsmen are Marines.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: In their hearts they are Marines.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: They were wonderful.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Immediately when I was hit, the corpsman was there, you know. As a matter of fact, the corpsmen saved my butt, too, in more ways than one. Because our corpsmen were armed with carbines and so were -- so was I. And the Chinese were coming in and I had to do some shooting, and I lifted my carbine and -- and -- and tried to fire off a few rounds and it would not fire. If you had even the slightest coating of oil on your weapons, with temperatures at 30 below zero, would -- would amalgamate the -- the thing so much that the weapon would not fire. Our corpsman was running by, and he was tending to our wounded, and I grabbed him, I said, "Does your carbine fire?" And he said, "Lieutenant, it fires one round at a time. It does not fire semiautomatic." I said, "Well, here, trade -- let me trade places with you and I'll -- let me give you -- let me use your carbine." So I used his carbine in terms of warding off the attack, and so the corpsman not only saved my butt in terms of tending to my wounds, but prior to that night he saved my butt in terms of fending off a few Chinese who were getting close to us. So. So, yeah. And Jim Davis (ph), who we got to know in -- in Florida, is a -- is an avid, avid Marine, but he's Navy to begin with but he's a corpsman. He -- he just loves the Marine Corps, you know, because for one thing the Marine Corps really saved his butt on a few occasions. He had -- he was wounded very severely one night, machine-gun fire. And he -- he couldn't make it. He couldn't crawl out, and so the Marines -- it was -- it was what took care of him. They said, "You know, we got to run and do the -- and do our attack." But he says -- but so they -- they kind of shunted him over into a ditch area and he said, "Don't worry." He said, the leader said, "We'll be back for you." So they put him in a ditch and he stayed there overnight, fortunately not bleeding to death. And, in fact, the next morning the Marines did come back and they did pull him up and get him on a truck and they did save his butt. And so he's eternally grateful that the Marines took care of him too. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: And he didn't bleed to death because it was so cold.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: And that's what saved him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: And 30 below is -- is pretty cold when you have --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: -- no place to go and nothing but open air, and maybe a cold rock to sit on perhaps. Yeah. Yeah. [END OF TRACK 1, BEGIN TRACK 2].

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there anything you could possibly do to keep warm?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Once in a blue -- [Interview cuts to the next section].

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: ___+ Dorothy Fuldheim's program. She was so irritated with herself because he used -- she asked him a few questions -- he used up the entire hour.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: And she -- you should have heard her moaning and groaning and complaining after that because he used up the entire time. But she said, it was so damn interesting, no wonder ---

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: But she was aggravated. {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah. But once in a while there'd be a fire started. Our sea rations were carried in -- in cardboard boxes, and the cardboard boxes were very heavy and they were very, very insulated. So when they had some sea rations to pass out, which were -- happen to be frozen solidly, then we could use sea ration as you tuck it under your armpit for a -- for a day or two, and maybe it'll thaw out to some extent. They -- they'd burn the cardboard boxes, and that fire lasted maybe ten or 15 minutes. And you had your brief moment of -- of respite. Yeah. Yeah. But it didn't last long. It was cold.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Incidentally, as an a little aside, as long as I'm -- I'm allowed to talk.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: The young man that he gave the liners to from his gloves, he turned out to be from the Cleveland area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: He did not know that at the time, and he was in some place, and all of a sudden this guy yelled, "There is the officer that saved my life." And it turned out to be a -- a boy from the Cleveland area, and he died like, what, about three years ago?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: So he did survive. And because -- and of course certainly because of the liners.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: I think that did help.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. {Whispers} What?

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You want a cookie? {Laughs}

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: No, thank you. No thanks. Thanks.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: You know, they're not real sweet, so they're good for in the morning. They're just kind of like a shortbread.

sp.speaker: Raymond R. Jorz
sp.p: But anyhow, yeah. Once a Marine always a Marine.
